#8048. Georgetown's Counterclaims Against Professor Fired for "Sexual Misconduct" Can Go Forward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Amy Berman Jackson (D.D.C.) yesterday in Egolf v. Georgetown Univ.:

Plaintiff David Egolf was a tenured associate professor at defendant Georgetown University …. In 2015, after an investigation into an internal complaint lodged against Egolf by a Georgetown student, the parties entered into a settlement agreement that placed rules on Egolf's conduct in return for his continued employment at the University. In 2023, following a second report by a recent Georgetown graduate, the University completed another investigation into Egolf and his conduct.

Egolf filed suit against Georgetown and certain University officials, claiming that the second investigation violated Title IX, Georgetown's Faculty Handbook, and the 2015 settlement agreement. Georgetown has answered the complaint and has filed a counterclaim alleging that Egolf breached the 2015 settlement agreement when he engaged in conduct that violated numerous provisions of the contract. Georgetown seeks compensatory damages and a declaratory judgment….

According to Georgetown, on September 20, 2013, a student accused Egolf of sexual harassment. Egolf was placed on administrative leave with pay while the University reviewed the student's complaint. The University's Office of Institutional Diversity, Equity, and Affirmative Action ("IDEAA") investigated the claim and, on May 9, 2014, issued a Notice of Findings in which it found, in part, that Egolf:

violated the University's Policy Statement on Harassment and Sexual Harassment by making unwelcome sexual advances and engaging in unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature in violation of the policy; engaged in prohibited retaliation against the student; and failed to recognize and ignored the principle underlying [the University's Policy on Consensual Sexual Relationships], which prohibits participation in a professional relationship with a student where there is a conflict of interest.

Moreover, with respect to the University's alcohol policy and Faculty Handbook, IDEAA found that:

(1) [Egolf] served, offered, gave, purchased, and provided alcohol on multiple occasions to [the student] and his roommate, both of whom were underage, and (2) [Egolf] engaged in unfair treatment of [the student], engaged in unprofessional conduct; abused his academic authority over [the student]; engaged in a personal relationship for his own gratification; improperly shared other student information with [the student]; and allowed his objectivity as a professor to be compromised.

The Notice of Findings recommended that the University consider "the most serious academic and employment sanctions," issue a no-contact directive between Egolf and the student, and require Egolf to remain off campus and have no contact with University students pending the University's decision regarding sanctions. Egolf appealed IDEAA's findings and recommendations, which were later upheld by the University's Equal Opportunity Examining Board on September 14, 2014.

According to Georgetown, on October 14, 2014, University Provost Robert Groves issued a Termination Letter to Egolf, and then on December 3, 2014, Egolf filed a Notice of Grievance challenging IDEAA's findings and Provost Groves's termination decision. After a closed and confidential conciliation process, on October 15, 2015, the parties entered into an agreement ("2015 Agreement") which permitted Egolf's reinstatement subject to "strict and continuing behavioral restrictions." The 2015 Agreement:

The 2015 Agreement also stated that if Egolf had "any questions as to whether a relationship with a student is appropriate," he was required to "immediately disclose the relationship to his chair or dean." …

In May 2023, Robert Roe, one of Egolf's former students, started a postbaccalaureate program at Georgetown under Egolf's supervision. While in school, Roe took multiple classes taught by Egolf, served as his Research Assistant over the course of a summer, and was his academic advisee. Georgetown alleges that, on or about July 19, 2023, Roe contacted defendant Samantha Berner, Georgetown's Title IX Coordinator and Director of Title IX Compliance, to raise concerns regarding Egolf's conduct, which Roe characterized as "grooming." …

According to Georgetown, on May 6, 2024, IDEAA released a confidential investigative report stating that there was "sufficient evidence under a preponderance of the evidence standard to substantiate a finding" of Egolf's sexual misconduct, resulting in violations of University policy, the Faculty Handbook, and the 2015 Agreement…. The IDEAA investigative report found that Egolf maintained a "personal and social relationship with a student that he advised, including frequent non-academic communications, social outings, private meetings, and sustained personal involvement extending beyond appropriate faculty-student boundaries." Egolf admitted the truth of certain factual findings in his appeal by stating, "[t]his statement is true," including:

According to Georgetown, in Egolf's appeal, he further admitted that he and Roe had meals together "about once a month" at a restaurant near the University where they would discuss academic and personal topics. The meals initially included other students and alumni but later became more often one-on-one. Egolf also allegedly admitted that:

[Egolf] invited Mr. [Roe] to spend the night at his house after their celebration of Mr. [Roe]'s graduation, since they expected to drink and it would be late. [Egolf] invited Mr. [Roe] to spend the night at his house after they went to see the Lion King so that he would not have to drive to Mr. [Roe]'s home in Reston and back the night immediately preceding when Mr. [Roe] was already slated to go to [Egolf]'s home for their graduation celebration.

According to Georgetown, Egolf stated in his appeal that he and the student consumed three-and-a-half bottles of champagne together that same evening; he left the door slightly ajar when he went into the bathroom; he told Roe stories about being propositioned by a student and finding a student naked on his couch; he made a joke about his college friend's genitalia; and he participated in conduct related to a drinking game.

Georgetown also alleges that Egolf provided Roe with private study sessions, inflated his grades in a manner inconsistent with academic evaluation standards, and substantially assisted in drafting a portion of his undergraduate thesis and grant application.

Moreover, Egolf allegedly texted Roe that, upon Roe's graduation, Egolf would be able to tell him "all of the crazy stories I've hinted at" and did share the explicit stories following graduation; engaged in discussions about nudity and other sexual topics; made a joke involving genitalia; and teased Roe while offering to help remove his pants. Finally, Georgetown alleges that Egolf failed to disclose the nature or extent of his relationship with Roe to any University administrator as required by the 2015 Agreement…..

Egolf was eventually fired. Before the firing (but after he was put on paid leave), he sued, alleging Title IX retaliation, breach of contract, and other matters, and Georgetown counterclaimed, "alleging breach of the 2015 Agreement and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing," and seeking compensatory damages for the costs of various proceedings (including the legal costs of defending the lawsuit). The court allowed the claims to go forward; an excerpt:

To state a claim for breach of contract, "it is enough for the plaintiff to describe the terms of the alleged contract and the nature of the defendant's breach." Contrary to Egolf's assertions, a plaintiff need not allege damages caused by the breach to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss…. Georgetown claims that Egolf violated the agreement by:

Finally, Georgetown identifies the five specific provisions of the 2015 Agreement they allege that Egolf violated.

Even if Egolf is correct that Georgetown must allege damages to state a claim, the Court does not find that, on the face of the counterclaim, consequential damages were outside the contemplation of the parties at the time of the contract…. [P]aragraph 11 of the Agreement demonstrates that the parties expressly contemplated the possibility of litigation. Ex. A at 11 ("Any breach, or actions taken upon breach, of the Agreement by either party may also be enforced by filing suit, or seeking an injunction, in a court of competent jurisdiction"). Resolving all reasonable inferences in Georgetown's favor, the Court does not find that legal damages were beyond the contemplation of the 2015 Agreement.

Brian Drockton and Henry Adam Platt (Saul Ewing LLP) represent Georgetown.

#8047. Judge releases DUI suspect after reading AI-assisted police report disclosure

An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report. (Image from Shutterstock)

An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report.

Anthony Edward Rene Quidera was arrested on Oct. 29 on charges of DUI, exceeding the 65 mph speed limit and possession of an open container.

Court records show that Quidera was driving his Dodge Charger over 100 mph on the interstate. The arrest report stated that the suspect’s car failed to maintain its lane and was driving on the left median shoulder. After Quidera was stopped, the trooper reported smelling alcohol on his breath.

The officer’s probable cause statement ended with the following disclosure: “This report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. The content reflects the officer’s own observations and recollections. All facts and statements are based solely on the officer’s account,” according to coverage by ABC15 Arizona.

According to Daniel Fenzel, the commissioner for the Maricopa County Superior Court in Arizona, he was “unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations made in the narrative (e.g., officer’s observations, signature of affiant officer) were authored, whether in whole or in part, by a generative AI.”

Fenzel’s release order stated that the court could not determine probable cause. After being released, Quidera did not show up for his Nov. 12 trial date, according to ABC15 Arizona.

#8046. Propane vs. Gas Generators: Pros and Cons

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 16, 2026 12:37 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Power outages are a common problem during thunderstorms, so it’s a good idea to have a backup plan ready to go when the lights go out. Gas and propane generators are common choices for home backup power, RV use, and camping trips.

Propane generators, for example, burn cleaner than gasoline generators, but tend to be more costly to purchase and operate. Gasoline generators are more efficient, but the fuel has a shorter shelf life and may not always be available in emergencies due to panic buying at local gas stations. This guide outlines other differences between the two that will help you decide which type of generator is right for your home.

Having a basic understanding of how the different types of generators work can help decide on the right choice for your home. A propane generator operates by burning the propane in an internal combustion engine. This process creates mechanical energy, which is used to turn a rotor within a magnetic field to generate electricity that can then be used to power appliances and other electronic devices.

Choosing a propane emergency generator for the home makes it easier to stockpile fuel for emergencies. Ken Goodrich, Founder and CEO of Kenerator, says “Propane is a great option for home backup power because it stores well and burns clean. Even when natural gas is temporarily shut off due to a natural disaster or infrastructure damage, a propane tank will continue to supply power.” Additionally, propane burns cleaner than gasoline, so you can expect the best propane generators to require less maintenance and produce fewer emissions.

Understanding how much propane a generator uses is key to deciding on the right model for your home, since propane generators tend to have lower fuel efficiency than gasoline generators. “Additionally, propane suppliers usually deliver to customers on a routine basis, so the homeowner needs to ensure they have enough propane to make it through an average outage,” notes Goodrich. It should also be mentioned that propane generators typically cost more up front and have higher operating costs, so they may not be the best choice for those looking for a cheap solution.

Whether you are looking to purchase a gas or propane generator, it’s good to know how the appliance operates. Generally, the operation of a gasoline generator can be described as a process that converts chemical energy into mechanical energy, which in turn produces electrical energy. More specifically, the engine burns gasoline to spin a shaft, which rotates magnets or electromagnetic fields near the stator, a stationary coil of wires. This induces a change in the magnetic field, creating an electrical current in the coils, that can then be used to power connected appliances and electrical devices.

The main benefit of a gas generator is that these appliances are more affordable to purchase and operate than propane generators, though there can be some fluctuation in the energy efficiency between specific models, so don’t hesitate to ask how much gas does a generator use when researching potential products.

Goodrich mentions that “portable gasoline generators are good options for camping and construction sites,” so you can make use of your generator even when you aren’t at home. Goodrich goes on to say that “gasoline generators are affordable, portable, easy to find, and simple to use,” making them a great choice for just about any home.

While gasoline generators may be cheaper to purchase and operate, gas does not burn as cleanly as propane, so there is a higher risk that these appliances will break down or require frequent maintenance to keep them in good condition. “Gasoline engines use carburetors, as opposed to mixers, which clog easily if not run on a weekly or monthly schedule,” Goodrich points out.

If you like the potential of both propane and gasoline generators, but can’t decide between one or the other, then you may find the best dual-fuel generators to be a good alternative. These generators work by switching between gasoline and propane using a manual or automatic fuel selector.

While the engine has the same combustion cycle for both fuels, it utilizes a built-in carburetor to atomize gasoline for combustion, but when using propane, the fuel passes through a separate external line and regulator before it is pulled into the engine by the vacuum created by the piston. Goodrich says that dual-fuel generators are “definitely a viable option. A lot of homeowners like having propane for its clean burn and long storage life, with gasoline as a backup if they run through their propane supply.”

Westinghouse iGen4500 has a 3.4-gal. gas tank that can run quietly for up to 18 hours; has a variety of ports but weighs 100+ lbs. Read the review.

Propane generators use safer, easier to store, and cleaner-burning fuel than gasoline generators; gas generators are more affordable to purchase and operate, with better fuel efficiency. “For most homeowners looking for reliable backup power, propane is the better long-term solution. That said, if you’re looking for something more budget-friendly, gasoline can still get the job done,” says Goodrich.

After gaining a basic understanding of the pros and cons between propane vs. gasoline generators, it’s a good idea to start your search by reading up on the best generator brands, then researching individual products that offer the features you want. Keep in mind that at the end of the day, a dual-fuel generator, powered by propane and natural gas, will offer you the best of both worlds so you are prepared for any emergency.

#8043. 14 Things You Can Do Now to Prepare for a Power Outage in Winter

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Jennifer Noonan, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Published Nov 16, 2026 5:18 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Power outages can be difficult to weather any time of year, but not having a working heater when temperatures are frigid can be hard on you and your home. When there’s a winter storm in the forecast, there’s no time to lose. If you start preparing for inclement weather now, even before there’s a whisper about bad weather, and you’ll be in better shape should blizzards, nor’easters, or bomb cyclones head your way.

Make sure you have a good supply of batteries (and if they’re rechargeable batteries, ensure that they’re fully charged!) in a range of sizes for all your emergency needs. Have spares ready for flashlights and radios as well as for smoke detectors, clocks, and other necessities that can run on battery backup.

How many times have you clicked on several flashlights in your junk drawer before finding one that actually works? Carefully test each of your flashlights and figure out which ones work and which don’t. Refresh the batteries and test them again, ditching the flashlights that still don’t work. Purchase additional flashlights if you need them (can you really have too many?). Make sure there’s a “good” light for each member of the family, at the very least. Don’t plan on using candles; flashlights are safer.

Always top off your cars’ fuel tanks when you’re expecting a big storm. Gas station pumps run on electricity and if the power goes out, you won’t be able to get gasoline. If you have a gas-powered portable generator, fill some gas cans, too, so you can keep the generator going.

A key component of a winter survival kit is a means of charging your mobile phone in your car, whether that’s a car charger for your phone or the right cord to connect auto to phone. With a full gas tank and a car charger, you’ll be able to keep your phone working even if you lose power for an extended period of time. You may also want to invest in a solar phone charger, which would allow you to charge your phone without sitting in your driveway.

If you have landline telephone service, it’s worth keeping an old corded landline phone around. Modern phones that plug into wall outlets will not work during a power outage, and having access to a usable landline will help you conserve your cell phone battery.

If the power goes out during winter, how will you keep warm? Devise a plan now, before you’re in that situation. Even a gas-powered furnace requires electricity to run the fan that sends warm air through the vents. If you have a gas fireplace, consider installing a battery backup for the starter if you don’t already have one. If you rely on a wood stove for heat, stock up on firewood. Do not use a propane heater inside the home unless it is one specifically designed for indoor use; carbon monoxide can build up and create a deadly hazard.

Mr. Heater’s Portable Buddy Heater quickly heats up to 225 sq. ft. of space and has a tip-over safety mechanism. Read the review.

When a heavy storm is in the forecast, stock up on drinking water, and fill up the bathtub and washing machine so you’ll have enough water for washing and for flushing the toilets. The PennState extension service says Americans use 50 to 100 gallons of water per person per day, but that kind of stockpile may be hard to achieve in an emergency situation. You will want to have on hand at least a gallon of potable water per person per day.

If your home relies on municipal water, your water taps will keep flowing in the event of a power outage. But homes on well water aren’t so lucky—well pumps won’t work without electricity.

How will you cook if you lose electricity? If you have gas appliances, you should be able to light the pilot light with a match if you lose power. But if you have an electric stovetop and oven, you won’t be able to use your stove. You can, however, use a propane grill or an open fire to cook outdoors. If that’s your plan, refill the propane tank, or buy a cord of wood. And whatever your appliance situation, make sure you have a manual can opener.

Lowering the temperature of your refrigerator and freezer before the storm hits will help them stay cooler longer if the power goes out, thus increasing the likelihood that your food will be safe to eat after the power outage. Consider moving perishables like milk and meat into the freezer so they’ll stay colder. To conserve the cold air inside, avoid opening the refrigerator doors more than you absolutely have to.

If a winter power outage lasts more than a few days, you may run out of fresh food (or a means to prepare food). For this reason, it’s a good idea to keep plenty of nonperishable foods with long shelf lives like nut butters, canned fruit and juices, granola bars, and crackers on hand to keep yourself nourished.

Radios may seem a relic of the past, but these old-fashioned devices may just save your bacon if you lose power for an extended period. When modern methods of emergency alerts such as TVs and phones are offline, an emergency radio with fresh batteries may be your lifeline to news and information about dangerous conditions, even evacuation alerts. Better yet, select a radio can be charged in multiple ways. The Eton Odyssey radio, for example, can be charged via hand crank, USB-C, solar, and rechargeable and alkaline battery.

The Midland WR120B can be programmed to check weather in 25 local regions, so you can stay on top of loved ones’ forecasts Read the review.

Loss of power could be an excuse for a fun “campout” in the living room. Ahead of the storm, make sure your tent and sleeping bags are in good shape, or acquire these items if you don’t have them. Ensure you have plenty of heavy blankets, too. Then, when the power is out and temps in the house drop, set up the tent and unroll the sleeping bags. Body heat from people together in an enclosed space will help keep everyone warm. And you’ll have a fun story to tell!

If you’ve been meaning to caulk your windows, do it before cold weather strikes. Check the weatherstripping around your doors; odds are it’s seen better days. If your budget allows, replace or supplement your attic insulation. A less expensive way of sealing out some cold is to purchase some door draft stoppers, which you can tuck away in a closet until they are needed.

The worst time to buy a generator is the day you need one. If you live in an area that frequently loses power, consider purchasing a portable power station or a backup generator, which can be switched on manually or can automatically kick in when the power goes out. You can get generators powered by gasoline, natural gas, propane, or diesel (or even dual-fuel or inverter generators); solar generators are also an option but of course require a solar setup too.

After Testing 20 Air Purifiers, We Found One That Does Something the Rest Can’t

Same functionality, different package? Not with this Sans air purifier, which offers more advanced filtration and features than most models I’ve tested—without a premium price tag.

#8042. The Best Dual-Fuel Generators for Home and Outdoor Use, Tested

Dual-fuel generators offer the flexibility to run on either gasoline or propane, making them a versatile option for backup power. But with so many available, and many costing over $1,000, we tested a range of top models to help you find the right fit. Based on our results, we chose the Westinghouse WGen9500DF as our top pick for its powerful output, multiple starting options, and wide selection of outlets.

If you’re considering a dual-fuel generator but aren’t sure how much power you need or which features matter most, this guide can help. Below, we explain what to look for and share how five of the best dual-fuel generators performed in our hands-on tests.

Bottom line: Dual-fuel generators offer flexibility and power for home and outdoor use. Our tests highlight the best models to suit various needs and budgets.

Multifuel generators use gasoline or propane to provide electric power to your home, campground, or jobsite. But before buying a dual-fuel generator, consider whether it will meet your needs.

One key aspect of dual-fuel generators is you cannot run them indoors since they produce toxic fumes. Instead, you must set them up outside in a sheltered location and provide electrical power to appliances through an extension cord.

They are relatively heavy, weighing 100 to 200 pounds on average, and typically loud, sometimes exceeding the acceptable volumes allowed at RV parks. An inverter generator may be a better choice if you want a quiet generator. These generators have an enclosed body and supply power using a computer-controlled inverter instead of a noisier alternator.

However, if you need a decent amount of power, can see yourself regularly using more than one fuel type, and can handle a little extra weight and noise, a dual-fuel generator may be right for you.

The following dual-fuel generators represent the best the market has to offer in various categories. BobVila.com team members thoroughly tested each one, and we detail their pros and cons below.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 4.5/5

When it comes to choosing a good all-around generator, it’s tough to beat the Westinghouse WGen9500DF. This powerful generator runs on gasoline or propane, and selecting one or the other is as simple as flipping a switch. The WGen9500DF comes with a 6.6-gallon gasoline tank that will power the unit for up to 12 hours at a 25 percent load.

Actual runtime will depend on gasoline quality and how much power you’re drawing. On propane, it can run up to 7 hours on a 20-pound tank when drawing a 50 percent load. This model has a 120/240V-50A outlet, a 120/240V-30A locking outlet, and four 120V-20A GFCI outlets. At 9,500 running watts on gasoline, it’s powerful enough to run several tools simultaneously as well as an oven/range combo and clothes dryer separately.

The downsides? At 211 pounds, this is a heavy generator. It’s also loud, comparable to a motorcycle, which is enough to annoy neighbors yet reasonable for its output. If you’re looking for a quiet model to use during a power outage, this might not be it. It is, however, a powerhouse of electrical output using whichever fuel is preferred.

What our tester says: “The remote-start key fob was my favorite feature—I could start the generator from a full 90 feet away once I put a fresh battery in the remote.” —Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Westinghouse dual-fuel generator at Amazon or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 5/5; Power 4.5/5; Value 4.5/5

After giving the recoil start a couple of pulls, we found that the engine came to life quickly. Our test rig included a couple of heat guns and hair dryers running simultaneously on different high and low settings to vary the load.

We found the generator handled 1,800 watts as advertised, but noise levels seemed louder than expected yet still in a reasonable range for output. Overall, this generator is a great option for light-duty needs such as small DIY projects and powering a couple of household appliances during an outage.

This Champion 7,500-watt dual-fuel generator is powerful enough to supply critical home circuits during an electrical outage or enough electricity for an off-grid DIY building site. Its startup is easy and intuitive, with a manual choke lever, an electrical start switch, and a recoil cord. During testing, it started on the first pull every time. Using gas, the Champion generator produces 9,375 starting and 7,500 running watts. A full 7.7-gallon tank will provide up to 10 hours of runtime at a 50 percent electrical load. On propane, it operates at 8,400 starting and 6,750 running watts, working for up to 5.5 hours on a 20-pound propane tank. It has two GFCI-protected duplex household outlets, a 120V-30A locking outlet, and a 120/240V-30A locking outlet.

We used the Champion at a building site to run a portable table saw, miter saw, pancake air compressor, router, and several battery chargers. The tools ran perfectly, and the generator didn’t lag. The only things we didn’t love about this generator were its fuel-guzzling nature and how difficult it was to transport. Its hard plastic wheels worked fine on pavement, but this 205-pound machine was not easy to roll across soft ground or lift into and out of our truck. For those looking to power an RV, be aware its 74 dB noise level will be too much for most campgrounds.

Get the Champion 7,500-watt dual-fuel generator at Blain’s Farm & Fleet.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 3/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 5/5; Power 4.5/5; Value 4/5

When it comes to portable generators, 12,000 watts is near the top end in terms of power. The DuroMax dual-fuel portable generator is a monster that can power several tools and appliances simultaneously without throwing a breaker. We tested the DuroMax using gasoline and propane. It can run up to 8 hours on a full 8.3-gallon gas tank when pulling a 50 percent load and up to 7 hours on propane at 50 percent capacity. It also has an electric starter and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that automatically shuts the generator down if it senses hazardous levels of CO gas.

The DuroMax comes with several plug-in ports that extend its usefulness. It has a 120V-30A outlet, a 120/240V-30A outlet, two 120V-20A outlets (for standard power cords), and one 120/240V-50A outlet. Though we liked its power, the DuroMax missed the mark in a few areas. It doesn’t have drop-down generator covers to protect the outlets, and it only has two 120V standard outlets. Like other gas-powered generators, it’s also loud. Overall, though, we found this generator powerful and easy to use, particularly at this price point.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 5/5

For a propane generator ready to go at a moment’s notice, the Wen DF11000T is a great option. This powerful generator produces 11,000 peak watts (required to start a powerful tool like a saw) and 8,300 running watts when using gasoline. It provides slightly less power when operating on propane–9,500 peak watts and 7,500 running watts–but that’s still a lot of electrical power.

After its initial break-in period, we rotated through several tests, using the Wen to power a chest freezer, full-size fridge-freezer, laptop, tankless water heater, shop lights, table, chop saw, and circ saw. It didn’t show signs of being under any load except for a split-second surge when we started up one of the saws (saws are notorious for drawing a lot of power on start-up). We tested all the tools and items we could think of and had no problems.

Then, we did it all again while running the Wen on propane. We got the same excellent results, and switching from gasoline to propane only required flipping a switch. This model comes with an electric start and has a large 6.6-gallon tank that will keep it running for up to 8.5 hours at a 50 percent load. It features four standard household outlets, a 30A outlet, and a 50A outlet.

Like many fuel-powered generators, the Wen is pretty loud, about as noisy as a lawn mower. Yet, based on our tests, that’s a small price to pay for the hefty amount of power this durable generator provides.

Get the Wen DF11000T dual-fuel generator at Amazon.

Before selecting several high-quality models for hands-on testing, we researched more than 24 dual-fuel generators, looking for quality construction, ease of use, portability, and power output. We gave some consideration to top manufacturers but didn’t automatically eliminate smaller or niche manufacturers if their generators were highly rated and competitively priced.

For actual testing, we assembled the generators and ran them according to the manufacturer’s instructions. We allotted time to models requiring break-in periods so the machines’ internal components could lubricate and settle before powering appliances or tools. Our team of testers then plugged in power tools, appliances, and more while using an online wattage calculator to estimate a suitable electrical load.

We awarded points to each model using a rubric considering ease of use, noise, portability, power, and value. The better a generator performed a test, the more points it received. After testing, we averaged the points to determine top performers.

To find the best dual-fuel generator for your home, campground, or worksite, consider the factors listed below, including fuel efficiency, fuel tank capacity, power output, and control panel configuration.

Dual-fuel generators have an isolated gasoline tank with a fuel capacity that ranges from as small as 2 gallons to more than 10 gallons. The larger the fuel tank on the generator, the longer the generator can provide gasoline-based power. But, as tank size increases, so does the size of the generator.

Fuel capacity does not affect how much propane you can use with your dual-fuel generator. Propane gas is stored under pressure in canisters, which attach to the generator with a hose and pressure regulator for direct fuel consumption.

The power output on dual-fuel generators is measured in watts. Manufacturers’ specs include peak power output and running power output. Peak power output refers to the maximum number of watts the generator can provide at any one time. Running power output equals the average number of watts produced during use.

Dual-fuel generators generally produce a power output from 1,000 watts to over 12,000 watts, depending on their size. Gasoline produces a higher wattage than propane, so many manufacturers of dual-fuel technology break wattage into propane peak and running outputs and gasoline peak and running outputs.

For greater power output needs, users may need to consider a standby generator rather than a portable dual-fuel option.

You can start your dual-fuel generator with an electric start switch or a recoil cord.

A generator’s operating noise level is measured in decibels. To understand the range of sound produced by a generator, consider these common sounds and their equivalent operating dB level:

Many dual-fuel generators produce 50 to 90 dB of noise, depending on fuel type (gasoline runs louder than propane) and power output. The most common range is between 65 dB and 75 dB, comparable to the sound of normal conversation.

The quietest dual-fuel generators combine dual-fuel technology and inverter technology to create a dual-fuel inverter generator.

Dual-fuel generators are typically large and heavy, with hoses or tanks that make them difficult to carry and move. Thus, some manufacturers include wheel kits for tilting the generator back and rolling it to the desired location.

You may also be able to purchase a wheel kit separately to add to your existing generator or replace an older wheel kit that doesn’t work well anymore. Either way, a wheel kit makes transporting a portable dual-fuel generator much easier.

Lift hook bars are handy on jobsites, allowing workers to attach the generator to a hook-and-pulley system and raise or lower it instead of carrying it up or down stairs or ladders. In industrial settings, this feature helps raise the generator onto a walkway or platform.

A lift hook bar will increase the generator’s weight (and likely the price), so don’t look for a generator with this feature unless you truly plan to use it.

Most dual-fuel generators are between 22 inches long by 22 inches wide by 22 inches high and 35 inches long by 30 inches wide by 30 inches high. They typically weigh between 100 and 250 pounds.

If you plan to move the generator frequently, figure size and weight prominently into your decision. Make sure the model you choose fits into your vehicle so you can transport it as needed. Remember, however, that larger, heavier motors are also the most powerful. You’ll want to find the right balance of size, weight, and power to meet your needs.

Gasoline and propane each have their pros and cons as fuel options. Gasoline is easier to find, but propane costs less. Propane is a better fuel source in hot summer weather, while gas burns better in the cold. A dual-fuel generator lets you choose one or the other based on immediate circumstances.

Using both fuel sources, one after the other, greatly increases a generator’s runtime. Users can run to the gas station to refuel while the generator keeps providing power on propane.

Before buying a dual-fuel generator, consider the answers to the following frequently asked questions.

A dual-fuel generator operates like a single-fuel generator, except it can burn propane and gasoline to produce electrical energy. It converts mechanical energy produced by the burning fuels to force the movement of electrical charges and generate electricity.

While some single-fuel generators can be adapted for use with natural gas, this isn’t the case with dual-fuel generators. Unless specially designed, dual-fuel generators do not run on natural gas and cannot be adapted for this purpose.

Propane gas is less expensive than gasoline, nearly impossible to spill, and burns cleaner, resulting in less wear on the engine over time. Running a dual-fuel generator on propane will save money but slightly decrease the machine’s peak and running watts.

Runtime is determined by fuel efficiency and fuel tank capacity. On average, a standard dual-fuel generator runs about 8 to 10 hours on propane.

If power is the goal, then the DuroMax dual-fuel generator is one of the best options to help ensure the campsite or essential home appliances have power for hours.

Depending on how much wattage a home draws under normal situations, attaching a high-capacity dual-fuel generator to its electrical system may be possible, but it’s not a DIY project.An electrician must install a transfer switch connecting the generator to the home’s electrical main. When the power goes out, the transfer switch automatically switches the incoming power from the grid to the generator. In most cases, the generator will be classified as a “standby generator” because it’s always ready to start generating electricity. Most portable generators are too small to run an entire home.

Generators running on gasoline are typically louder than those running on propane since burning propane requires less energy.

As with most outdoor tools and large household appliances, you will want to take dual-fuel generators to a local recycling plant for recycling.

#8041. The Pew Research Center Report on Future of World Religions

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The religious landscape in the United States will look very different in 2070, and so will debates about religious liberty.

The Pew Research Center has published a comprehensive survey about population growth within the world religions between 2020 and 2070. The results are worth a careful study to forecast the future religious landscape in the United States, and how those numbers will affect debates about religious liberty. Here is a summary:

The United States is expected to follow roughly the same pattern of religious change as the overall North American region.5 By 2070, Christians are expected to decline to less than half of the U.S. population, while religiously unaffiliated people will rise to about 41%. And Jews – who were the country's third-largest religious group in 2020 – will be outnumbered by both Muslims and Hindus in 2070 if recent demographic trends continue.

The numbers concerning Jews are also significant:

As of 2020, Pew Research Center estimates there were about 15 million Jews by religion around the world, 12.5 million of whom lived in Israel and the United States. By the Center's projections, Israel alone will hold the majority of the world's Jews within a few decades.

If recent demographic trends continue, Israel will be home to 62% of the global Jewish population in 2070, up from 46% in 2020. During this 50-year time span, the number of Jews living in Israel is forecast to grow from 6.8 million to 11.1 million, due primarily to what demographers call "natural increase": the number of births exceeding the number of deaths in a population.

I've written on this blog before that I can see a future where my family and I will have to move to Israel. The events of the last election make that outcome seem just-that-much-more likely. And remember, the persecution of Jews will always be a precursor to persecution of other faiths.

Ultimately, debates about religious liberty will look very different as the composition of religious group changes. I would note that at the recent Federalist Society convention, there was a brief mention about the risks of Shariah Law--a topic that I can't ever recall being discussed on a FedSoc platform. This issue will soon get even hotter in Texas as the government continues to shift.

There are also outdoor Christmas light projectors, which aren’t Christmas lights in a traditional sense, but they can add a festive flair to a holiday display.

Outdoor Christmas lights come in various lengths, from 10 feet to 100 feet or more. Measure the distance the lights will need to cover to get an idea of the right number of strings for the lighting design, accounting for any swag or draping for effect. Falling a few feet short can easily impact your outdoor Christmas display.

If you’re considering an outdoor Christmas light projector, remember the area the display can cover is explicitly defined in terms of square footage. While you can move the projector farther from the house to expand the display size, that may affect the quality of the images and the density of the colors it displays.

Electricity and solar are the main power sources for outdoor Christmas lights, though you can also sometimes find battery-operated Christmas lights. Of the two, electricity is by far the more reliable. Electricity provides consistent power, though it also requires extension cords and access to an outdoor outlet in the right location.

Solar-powered Christmas lights are less common but are still a viable option. They’re an energy saver, generating energy via a solar panel during the day, but they aren’t without their flaws. The biggest problem is power consistency. Solar power must be stored to keep the lights running after the sun goes down. Many of these lights shine brightly for about 1 or 2 hours but then dim as power fades. Yes, they save power, but they’re not nearly as bright or consistent as electric lights.

LED Christmas light bulbs use light-emitting diodes instead of filaments like incandescent bulbs. The diodes require less energy and last longer than filaments, creating a long-lasting, energy-efficient light bulb. LED lights also remain cool to the touch, reducing the risk of fire. Outdoor LED Christmas lights come in a wider variety of colors than incandescent ones. When paired with smart features, they can create a rainbow of options.

Even if you’ve been helping with outdoor Christmas lights since you were a kid, you might still have a few questions about this particular category of string lights. Our answers to the following frequently asked questions can help you get your lights selected and installed so that your home looks its best this holiday season.

When hanging outdoor Christmas lights, recruit a helper, get a sturdy ladder, and prepare for at least a few hours of work. Start with a string near an electrical outlet and hang your Christmas lights by following the roofline. Have your helper hold the ladder for stability. If the lights you’re hanging don’t have clips, you can attach them with nails, a staple gun, or removable light clips. Of these options, the removable clips are easiest and cause the least damage to the home.

Unlike indoor Christmas lights, outdoor Christmas lights should be 100 percent waterproof. If they’re not, they could short out the first time it rains or snows. Check the IP rating, which consists of two digits. The first number indicates dust and debris resistance, and the second indicates water resistance on a scale of 0 to 9. Waterproof outdoor Christmas lights should have a rating of at least 4 (in the second digit) or higher. Lights with a 4 or 5 can resist light rain, though they may not do well in extremely wet weather.

Yes, Christmas outdoor lights are safe to leave on all night. However, you might want to connect them to a timer to save energy.

Yes, LED outdoor Christmas lights last longer than older-style bulbs. The U.S. Department of Energy says that LED bulbs last up to 25 times longer than incandescent bulbs.

The size of bulbs you choose for your outdoor Christmas lights depends mostly on your personal preferences. In our tests, we really liked the look of Noma’s C9 Christmas Lights on our roofline and mini lights like the Prextex White Wire Lights wrapped around our covered porch’s beams.

Some outdoor lighting will have a control box near its plug that isn’t waterproof and must be covered or otherwise kept out of the elements. Other options for outdoor Christmas lights will be fully waterproof, as stated on the packaging.

Choosing the best color for outdoor Christmas lights is 100 percent personal preference, so pick whichever color or colors you prefer! If you’re looking to change colors this year and want to responsibly part ways with old lights, see our guide on recycling Christmas lights for more information.

Like color and size, brightness for outdoor Christmas lights mostly comes down to personal preference. Cool white lights may be best for you if you prefer something on the brighter end of the spectrum. Colored or warm white options typically aren’t quite as bright.

LexLab, the legal technology hub at the University of California College of the Law at San Francisco, is launching a three-day artificial intelligence legal tool building course, Law & AI Certificate Lab.

The intensive LAIC Lab course, offered Dec. 1-3, is a condensed, intensive version of one offered to law students over the course of a semester, offering lawyers and leaders a deep dive into the logic underlying legal AI while offering hands-on exploration of AI systems.

The course allows students to work with AI company Legora and AI platform Harvey as well as Replit, an app and website builder.

At the end of the certificate program, students should be able to move beyond using “chat” to build repeatable playbooks, checklists and other workflows; evaluate AI tools and vendors; determine whether tech should be bought or built; and manage privilege, confidentiality, conflicts and competence issues in AI-augmented practice.

#8037. Expressly Christian Messages by Secretary of Agriculture to Employees Violated Establishment Clause,

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Trina Thompson (N.D. Cal.) today in Nat'l Federation of Federal Employees v. U.S. Dep't of Agriculture:

The Court ORDERS that the Secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages. She "[m]ust stop if a colleague asks [her] to stop," she "[c]annot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances," and she "[c]annot use official authority to pressure subordinates." USDA Secretary's Memorandum 1078-019. She may "[d]iscuss [her] religious beliefs with interested colleagues," "[s]hare why [her] faith is meaningful to [her]," "[p]olitely invite coworkers to religious services or events," "[e]xpress religious viewpoints during appropriate conversations." This Court expresses no view whatsoever on what the Secretary can and cannot do in her personal capacity….

On July 4, 2025, Secretary [of Agriculture Brooke] Rollins sent an email from her official email account celebrating Independence Day. The message was sent to all USDA employees. Her message concluded with a written statement, "May God continue to protect the United States of America and may His favor shine over all her land." On November 26, 2025, Rollins sent a Thanksgiving message from her official email account to all USDA employees, attributing the first Thanksgiving in part to "gratitude towards a loving God."

The complaint identifies two subsequent communications as expressly promoting Christianity. On December 23, 2025, Rollins emailed USDA employees a Christmas message containing a video in which she stated that "The spirit of generosity flows from the very first Christmas when God gave us the greatest gift possible, the gift of his Son and our Savior Jesus Christ, who came to free us from our sins and open the door to eternal life. This is the reason for the season…."

On April 5, 2026, she sent an Easter email addressed to "All USDA Employees" which read:

Today we celebrate the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind.

From the foot of the Cross on Good Friday to the stone rolled away from the now empty tomb, sin has been destroyed. Jesus has been raised from the dead. And God has granted each of us victory and new life. And where there is life — risen life — there is hope.

No matter the very real trials and hardships we face, fear and sin and death do not get the last word. Because on Easter morning, "Hell took a body, and discovered God. It took earth, and encountered Heaven. It took what it saw, and was overcome by what it did not see." Now that is reason to rejoice!

And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for.

Please know how amazed and grateful I am for the hard work each of you do to support our shared mission here at USDA. I hope you and your loved ones have a truly blessed and happy Easter. May God continue to bless you, your families, and our exceptional country, One Nation, Under God.

At the top of the email, Secretary Rollins included an illustration of a stone rolled away from Jesus' tomb with the words "Christ is Risen" written above the illustration.

Plaintiffs allege that Rollins has not sent comparable messages acknowledging other religions' holidays. They contrast her communications with USDA's November 20, 2025 guidance on religious expression, which provides that officials "[c]annot use official authority to pressure subordinates" regarding religious beliefs and "[m]ust stop if a colleague asks [them] to stop." They further allege that Rollins defended the Easter message publicly and is likely to send similar communications marking future Christian holidays.

Each individual plaintiff received and read the challenged messages. Plaintiffs allege that they are expected to read communications from the Secretary because those communications may contain consequential workplace information. Other messages have addressed agency reorganization, employee relocation, changes to USDA's civil rights program, shutdown planning, and the Deferred Resignation Program; holiday messages have historically included administrative-leave announcements.

The individual plaintiffs allege that the messages convey a preference for employees who share the Secretary's Christian beliefs, make them feel excluded, and pressure them to conceal their own beliefs or appear to share hers. They fear workplace disfavor and retaliation for objecting; the complaint also alleges that supervisors have warned that objections would result in "trouble." Plaintiff Poopatanapong alleges that she no longer feels safe discussing a Buddhist holiday she celebrates; Roberts, an atheist, feels silenced; and Wolfe, a Pagan, feels pressure to appear Christian to advance professionally. alleges that its USDA members likewise received the messages, felt compelled to read them, and experienced pressure to accept the Secretary's beliefs while withholding their own.

The court held that plaintiffs' Establishment Clause were likely violated:

The Establishment Clause protects religious freedom by "command[ing] a separation of church and state." Kennedy v. Bremerton Sch. Dist., 597 U.S. 507, 558–59 (2022) (citing Cutter v. Wilkinson, 544 U.S. 709, 719 (2005)). [Note that this quote is actually from Justice Sotomayor's dissent in Kennedy, though it appears in the Cutter majority. -EV] At its core, this means forbidding "sponsorship, financial support, and active involvement of the sovereign in religious activity." As the Supreme Court acknowledged in Kennedy, the Establishment Clause does not "'compel the government to purge from the public sphere' anything an objective observer could reasonably infer endorses or 'partakes of the religious.'" However, courts must be cautious to ensure that "what might begin as a tolerant expression of religious views" does not "end in a policy to indoctrinate and coerce."

To determine whether government action violates the Establishment Clause, the Court must "focus[ ] on original meaning and history" of the First Amendment. That is, this Court's must be guided by "historical practices and understandings" of the relationship between government and religion in America. Pursuant to this approach, any practice that was "accepted by the Framers and has withstood the critical scrutiny of time and political change" does not violate the Establishment Clause. The analysis does not end merely because a practice has been observed in the past. The history and tradition test requires this Court to look to the "uninterrupted practice" of law in our nation's traditions.

Traditionally, the hallmark of government conduct violative of the Establishment Clause is the presence of some form of coercion upon its citizens.

Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, the two Founders most instrumental in the drafting and ratification of the Religion Clauses of the First Amendment, articulated a founding-era concern broader than direct, compelled sectarian practices. Madison, for example, expressed concern that even instances of governmental "recommendation[]" concerning religion "naturally terminate[] in a conformity to the creed of the majority []." Jefferson expressed concern about indirect forms of coercion such as conduct which might invite "some degree of proscription perhaps in public opinion." Most fitting, in his "Memorial and Remonstrance Against Religious Assessments" drafted in 1785, Madison questioned the ends sought by the promotion of a sectarian underpinning to our country's political foundation: "Who does not see that the same authority which can establish Christianity, in exclusion of all other Religions, may establish with the same ease any particular sect of Christians, in exclusion of all other Sects?" His guidance, contained in the same writings: "Such a Government will be best supported by protecting every Citizen in the enjoyment of his Religion with the same equal hand which protects his person and his property; by neither invading the equal rights of any Sect, nor suffering any Sect to invade those of another." The Founders may have lacked the foresight to account for contemporary technological advances, but the principles embedded in our First Amendment ring as true today. As difficult as the task may be, below, this Court faithfully applies the founding-era's understanding of the Establishment Clause to the modern-day circumstances giving rise to this litigation….

After reviewing and weighing the Establishment Clause jurisprudence, the Court finds that Secretary Rollins appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion. Here, three factors inform the Court's conclusion that the Secretary's conduct was coercive: (1) her position of authority, (2) the use of her official email to send messages to all USDA employees, and (3) the alienating language contained in the emails to employees who did not share her religious tenets. [Detailed discussion of factors 1 and 2 omitted for space reasons. -EV]

It makes no difference that the emails did not single out dissidents, disparage those who did not share the Secretary's beliefs, or indicate work-related decisions would be influenced by an employees' reaction to the emails. The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that "immense social pressure" can result in a finding of coercion. Such pressure is demonstrated here…. While social pressure alone is not state coercion because "mature adults … presumably are not readily susceptible to religious indoctrination or peer pressure[,]" the totality of the circumstances here demonstrates such immense pressure to amount to coercion….

The Court does not purport to regulate the religiosity of the Secretary—nor could it. "A relentless and all-pervasive attempt to exclude religion from every aspect of public life could itself become inconsistent with the Constitution." Nor does this Court generally condemn the expression of religious sentiments. Instead, this Court requires the Secretary to observe her own directives. USDA Secretary's Memorandum 1078-019. The April 5, 2026, and December 23, 2025, messages go too far. They suggest acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure; a pressure of conformity sufficient to raise an Establishment Clause violation….

NEXT: The Pew Research Center Report on Future of World Religions

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#8033. The 10 Best Ways to Use Your Grandma’s Favorite $5 Cleaner

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Rachelle Dragani, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Published Nov 17, 2026 4:07 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

As a gas, ammonia, hydrogen and nitrogen chemical compound is pungent and dangerous. But in its diluted household form, the nitrogen-based super cleaner is a workhorse in the war on common household dirt and grime. Ammonia is readily available, inexpensive, and potent, so a little goes a long way.

Before you buy ammonia, know that there are various types of household ammonia to choose from. You may see “cloudy” or “sudsy” versions—that’s ammonia with soap added, which is generally used for such domestic cleaning chores as treating stained clothing or scrubbing stovetops. We recommend opting for “clear” ammonia, which is suited to a wider variety of tasks (and you can always add a tablespoon or two of dish soap to make clear ammonia sudsy). You’ll also find ammonia that’s scented with lemon or pine to temper its stinging odor.

The harsh smell serves as a warning, though: Working with ammonia absolutely requires caution. Pure chemical ammonia can cause severe burns and respiratory issues if it comes into contact with skin or is ingested. Even diluted in water, as is recommended for most cleaning purposes, ammonia can still be harmful.

Mixing ammonia and chlorine bleach creates a toxic gas called chloramine. Take great care not to combine them—doing so could have dire consequences.

The most important safety rule to remember is: Never mix ammonia with chlorine bleach. The result is a highly toxic chlorine gas that can produce headaches, seizures, and other symptoms. It’s crucial to keep this in mind if you’re using ammonia with laundry or to clean surfaces. You want to make absolutely sure not to mix it with a detergent or household cleaner that contains bleach.

When using ammonia, be sure to wear chemical-resistant gloves and ventilate the area well. Be sure, too, to store it where pets and children can’t access it. Bearing these safety guidelines in mind, put ammonia to work around the home, as generations have done before us.

To achieve streak-free mirrors, windows, and crystal, mix 1 tablespoon clear ammonia with 2 cups water in a spray bottle. Spritz the solution onto glass items and wipe immediately with a soft, lint-free cloth for windows and crystal; paper towels work fine for mirrors.

To remove stains on a concrete driveway, garage floor, or patio, mix 1 cup ammonia with 1 gallon of water in a bucket and apply it to the stain with a mop or large sponge. Let sit for about 20 minutes, and then scrub the stain with a bristled brush. Rinse the surface with clean water. If the stain isn’t completely gone after the area dries, repeat the process until you’re satisfied with the results.

If gold, silver, diamond, or platinum jewelry has lost its shine, mix 6 parts warm water to 1 part ammonia in a bowl (one that you don’t eat or cook with and add your jewelry. (Never use ammonia to clean pearls or other gems.) After 15 minutes, remove the jewelry with your gloved hand, and then gently scrape away any stubborn grime with a soft-bristled toothbrush (one that’s no longer in use or designated for cleaning). Allow it to soak for another 15 minutes, remove from the solution, and immediately rinse with warm water. Dispose of used ammonia solution down the drain while running the hot water. Polish the jewelry with a soft, lint-free cloth and let it dry.

Stubborn stains on cotton, polyester, or nylon fabrics are no match for a solution of ⅔ cup clear ammonia, ⅔ cup dish soap, 6 tablespoons of baking soda, and 2 cups warm water. Mix in a bowl or bucket and apply generously to stains with a sponge or spray bottle. Let the treatment sit for about 30 minutes, then launder as usual. For tougher stains like blood or grass, treat the stain again with a solution of 1 part ammonia and 1 part warm water.

Note: Do not use ammonia on wool or silk, which can eat through the delicate fabrics. And remember never to mix ammonia with any laundry products that contain bleach.

Tackle caked-on grease on stove burners with this trick. Place each burner in a separate sealable plastic bag filled with ¼ cup ammonia. Seal each bag to keep fumes at bay, and place in a sink or washtub for 8 to 12 hours. Open the bags in a ventilated area, and remove all grease and dirt easily with a quick scrub of dish soap and water. Once the gunk is gone, thoroughly rinse the burners with water to get rid of ammonia residue. Let dry completely before using.

Mix one part clear ammonia and one part hot water in a sprayer or other bottle. Apply generously to the stain by spritzing or with a sponge. After about 10 minutes of dwell time, place a clean old towel over the stain and press with an iron, blasting with steam, for about 20 seconds. Check your progress: The stain should start transferring to the towel. Repeat, with steam ironing and more ammonia solution if needed, until the stain is gone.

Ammonia is tough on every odor from fresh paint to burnt lasagna. Place a small container filled with about 1/2 cup of clear ammonia near an offending smell, being sure to keep the area ventilated, to absorb the nastiness within hours.

Heat the oven to 150 degrees, and set a large pot of water on the stove to boil. Turn off the oven and open the windows to ventilate the kitchen. Place a sturdy container, such as a glass measuring cup or metal bowl, filled with ½ cup ammonia on the oven’s top shelf. Place the pot of boiled water on the bottom shelf. Close the oven and let sit for 8 to 12 hours, then remove the containers of ammonia and water. Open the oven door and air air out for at least an hour before cleaning. Because the grime has basked in ammonia fumes, it should be loosened and easy to remove with a sponge, warm water, and dish soap.

This method is only recommended for electric ovens, because mixing ammonia with gas can be dangerous. If you choose to use this method on your gas oven, make sure that the pilot light and gas lines are turned off.

To clean and disinfect kitchen and bath tiles, mix ¼ cup ammonia with 1 gallon of water in a bucket and use a sponge or mop to liberally apply the solution to the tile. Use a soft-bristled brush to scrub any particularly stubborn areas. Finish up by rinsing the surface with clean water and your sponge or mop.

Ammonia’s strong scent can deter unwanted critters. Fill a saucer with clear, unscented ammonia, or saturate a rag or cotton balls with it. Then place in areas that attract pests, such as near garbage cans where raccoons prowl or beside cracks in the basement where mice enter. The smell will remind the varmints of predators, so they’re likely to catch a whiff and turn away, unharmed. That said, make sure to keep the ammonia deterrent out of reach of kids and pets.

So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. #8031. Retrospective Voting and the 2026 Election

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A key "information shortcut" worked well in the 2026 election. But political ignorance remains a serious danger.

In my book Democracy and Political Ignorance  and various other writings going all the way back to my very first academic article (published in 1998), I have warned of the dangers of widespread voter ignorance. And I have argued that "information shortcuts" - small bits of knowledge that supposedly make up for ignorance about details - are generally ineffective or even counterproductive. Thus, I should acknowledge that one of those shortcuts - retrospective voting - worked fairly well in the recently concluded 2026 election. At the same time, the problem of political ignorance remains a grave menace.

Retrospective voting is probably the most often-used information shortcut, and the one most cited by scholars who argue that voter ignorance isn't much of a problem. The basic idea is simple: to be a good voter you don't need to know much about government and public policy. You just need to know whether things are going well or badly under the rule of the incumbents.

If things are going well, you vote to reelect them to continue their good work. If badly, you vote to "throw the bastards out." Then you elect a new set of bastards in their place; but the new bastards will hopefully know they need to do a good job, else they will get thrown out in their turn, at the next election. As Ronald Reagan famously put it during the 1980 election, "Next Tuesday all of you will go to the polls… I think when you make that decision it might be well if you would ask yourself: Are you better off than you were four years ago?"

I and other critics have long pointed out that, when ignorant voters use the retrospective voting shortcut, they often end up rewarding and punishing incumbents for things they did not cause (usually short-term economic trends), while ignoring more subtle long-term issues. In addition, they often don't know which officials are responsible for which issues, and tend to overlook the possibility that the opposition party's policies will be as bad or worse.

Nonetheless, retrospective voting actually worked pretty well in the 2026 election. As I noted in a previous post, polls show that many voters punished the Republicans for high prices caused by Trump's tariffs,  the failed Iran War, and the administration's cruel campaign of mass deportations (which particularly angered Hispanic voters in key states and congressional districts). One can also add the issue of corruption, which polls  indicate also had a big impact.

The Republicans really were responsible for all three of these policies. They weren't caused by exogenous factors outside of Trump's control. And the policies really did have massive negative effects in raising prices, an unsuccessful war, and massive cruelty and violations of civil liberties caused by the deportation campaign. The scope and effects of corruption are harder to measure. But this administration may be the most corrupt in American history. And, on all four issues, the Democrats are likely to be at least somewhat better.

But while retrospective voting worked reasonably well in the 2026 midterm election, we cannot conclude that the problem of political ignorance doesn't matter, or even that it's overblown. Rather, the shortcut was effective primarily because of the large and obvious nature of Trump's failures.

Along with other scholars, I have long recognized that retrospective voting can be effective if incumbents screw in ways that have large and obvious bad effects - ones that even very ignorant voters can easily see and understand. For example, I often cite economist Amartya Sen's famous finding that mass famines never or almost never occur under democracies (even as they happen much more often under dictatorships). Even ignorant voters will notice a famine is going on, blame incumbents for it, and vote accordingly.

Trump's failures over the last two years weren't quite as bad as a mass famine. But they were nonetheless large (including a major war and  the highest tariff schedule since the Great Depression), highly visible, and many of their effects were easy to understand. It isn't hard to notice that massive tariff increases cause prices to rise. The war and its effects on prices were also highly visible. Images of brutal deportations and resulting civil liberties violations were all over the news. Most voters probably didn't know about the details of the administration's corruption. But there was so much of it, that most probably heard at least something about it.

Many policy failures are far less readily apparent than that. And ignorant voters are therefore likely to overlook or misunderstand them. It's not hard to find examples even in the 2026 election itself. To take a particularly important case, the US faces a massive looming fiscal crisis, caused in large part by the combination of an aging population and out-of-control entitlement spending.  Yet most candidates of both parties largely ignored this problem, and promise continued massive spending, and avoiding tax increases for almost everyone, except perhaps a few billionaires and other very wealthy people. They could do that because surveys show most voters are ignorant about our fiscal situation and especially don't realize the key role of entitlement spending.

Voters' justified negative reaction in 2026 to tariffs, mass deportations, corruption, and the Iran War also highlight the failure of information shortcuts in the 2024 election. At that time, it was evident to informed observers that Trump would seek to institute massive tariffs and cruel deportation policies. Indeed, I myself was among those who cited them as among the principal reasons to oppose Trump in that election. Large-scale corruption was also predictable, given Trump's long history of skullduggery. Yet swing voters got these issues wrong - despite the fact that high prices were a major issue in 2024, and tariffs and mass deportations would predictably raise them (as I also pointed out at the time).

The Iran War was admittedly less predictable. Trump even promised to avoid new wars. But his well-documented combination of ignorance and impulsiveness meant that returning him to office created a significant risk of a foreign policy crisis spiraling out of control.

And on all these issues, it was predictable (and predicted by many, including me) that Trump 2.0 would surround himself with cronies and loyalists likely to indulge his worst instincts. No longer would he be constrained by "adults in the room," as occasionally happened during his first term.

Thus, while an information shortcut worked well in 2026, it's important to recognize that was only necessary because shortcuts failed miserably in 2024, which was an only modestly more difficult situation. In that earlier election, we did not yet see the effects of Trump's awful second-term policies. But most of those policies and effects were readily predictable by any moderately well-informed observer. Yet most swing voters were much more ignorant than that, and thus instead voted to punish Democrats for high prices, ignoring the high likelihood that electing Trump would make that problem worse, not better.

In addition, as I emphasized in my November 2024 post on voter ignorance in that year's election, a combination of ignorance and bias led many voters to underestimate the significance of Trump's assault on basic norms and principles of liberal democracy.

It is also important to remember that the problem of voter ignorance is not just that it leads voters to make "wrong" choices between the options put before them. It also makes those options worse in the first place. As I have long argued in my book and elsewhere, political ignorance also makes those options worse in the first place. Politicians and campaign strategists know they face a largely ignorant electorate, and act accordingly. Sweeping the fiscal crisis under the rug is just one of many examples of that tendency. Even if information shortcuts consistently helped voters choose the lesser of the evils before them (which, sadly, they don't!), ignorance would still make those options much more evil than they would be otherwise.

Trump is a particularly egregious long-time exploiter of political ignorance, which played key roles in his rise and return to power. But more conventional politicians also routinely exploit it, as Barack Obama did, for example.  For those keeping score, I have been arguing that political ignorance is a serious danger for over 25 years, under both Republican and Democratic administrations, and through many changes in the political winds.

The  2024 election led me to conclude that voter ignorance was an even more serious problem than I previously thought. This year's election is, perhaps, a data point for the other side.  But whether or not the problem is worse than I thought before 2024, it continues to be a serious danger.

There is no easy fix for widespread voter ignorance. I assessed  various possible options in my 2023 book chapter on "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance, and in Chapters 5-7 of Democracy and Political Ignorance. I think the most promising approach make fewer decisions at the ballot box and more by "voting with your feet," where incentives to seek out information and use it wisely are better. I also argue in both works that the idea of simply paying voters to increase their knowledge deserves more attention. But any remedy will take time, and we may need a combination of several strategies, not just one.

In sum, the 2026 election is an example of retrospective voting working relatively well. But we should not conclude this shortcut - or any other - is a good general solution to the problem of widespread political ignorance.

NEXT: Expressly Christian Messages by Secretary of Agriculture to Employees Violated Establishment Clause,

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.
